title: WordPress dbDelta Custom Table Schema and Migration Standards
description: WordPress utilizes dbDelta() for declarative schema creation and atomic migrations. dbDelta enforces strict formatting rules: exact spacing, capitalized keywords, and explicit primary key declarations are mandatory for error-free execution.
rules: Include require_once( ABSPATH . 'wp-admin/includes/upgrade.php' ) before executing dbDelta().
Each field definition must be on its own line in the CREATE TABLE statement.
PRIMARY KEY definition must have exactly two spaces after 'PRIMARY KEY' (e.g. 'PRIMARY KEY  (id)').
Use KEY instead of INDEX for secondary indexes, and specify indexed columns in parentheses.
SQL keywords (CREATE TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, DEFAULT, AUTO_INCREMENT, KEY) must be strictly UPPERCASE.
Use $wpdb->get_charset_collate() for table character sets and collation compatibility.
Store the installed schema version in wp_options to prevent redundant dbDelta execution on standard page requests.
anti_patterns: Using single space after PRIMARY KEY: 'PRIMARY KEY (id)' (causes dbDelta to fail or re-create index every run).
Writing multiple field definitions on a single line.
Using backticks on data types or lowercase keywords like 'create table'.
Running dbDelta() on every 'init' hook instead of plugin activation or version-upgrade gates.

title: Custom Tables vs. wp_postmeta & wp_options Architecture Matrix
description: High-volume, transactional, and structured relational data must use custom database tables rather than postmeta or options to prevent database bloat, slow non-indexed queries, and autocommit performance degradation.
rules: Use Custom Database Tables for high-frequency records (> 10,000 entries), event logs, financial transactions, commission ledgers, and analytics tracking.
Use Custom Post Types (CPT) + Postmeta for user-editable content nodes that require standard WordPress REST APIs, Gutenberg block editing, revision tracking, or admin edit screens.
Use wp_options strictly for global plugin settings, feature flags, and schema version numbers (avoid storing large unbounded arrays).
Always prefix table names using $wpdb->prefix to respect multisite and custom installation prefixes.
anti_patterns: Storing thousands of high-velocity tracking events or analytics clicks in wp_postmeta.
Querying meta_key and meta_value with complex mathematical aggregations (e.g. SUM(meta_value)) without indexes.
Storing large unbounded growing logs in wp_options with autoload='yes' (causes entire site memory bloat on every request).
